chunks.title: What the Internet of Things is
chunks.content: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical objects, called things, that have sensors, software and network connectivity so they can collect data and exchange it with other devices and systems over the internet. Each thing needs a unique identity, such as an IP address or a device ID, so that it can be found and addressed. Things sense their environment, for example temperature, motion or light, and some can also act on it through actuators such as motors, valves or switches. Key characteristics of IoT are connectivity, sensing, unique identity, heterogeneity (devices from many vendors with different hardware and protocols), very large scale (billions of devices) and dynamic change, because devices join, leave, move or sleep to save energy. Many IoT devices are constrained: they have little memory, low processing power and run on batteries.

chunks.title: Applications of IoT
chunks.content: IoT is used in many sectors. In smart homes, connected lights, thermostats, door locks and cameras can be monitored and controlled from a phone, and rules can automate them, such as turning off lights when nobody is in a room. In agriculture, soil moisture sensors tell an irrigation system when to water crops, which saves water. In healthcare, wearable devices track heart rate or blood glucose and can alert doctors remotely. In industry, sensors on machines measure vibration and temperature to predict failures before they happen, which is called predictive maintenance. In smart cities, IoT supports smart parking, street lights that dim when roads are empty, and air quality monitoring.

chunks.title: Challenges of IoT
chunks.content: IoT also brings challenges. Security is a major one: many devices ship with default passwords and rarely get software updates, so attackers can take them over, for example to build a botnet. Privacy is another, because sensors in homes and wearables collect personal data about people's habits and health. Interoperability is hard because devices from different vendors use different protocols and data formats, so they cannot always work together; standards and gateways help. Energy is limited for battery-powered devices, so they must use low-power hardware and radios and sleep most of the time. Scalability matters because a system may have to manage millions of devices and handle large volumes of data.

chunks.title: Components of an IoT system
chunks.content: A typical IoT system has several components. Sensors measure physical quantities such as temperature, humidity or motion, and actuators change the physical world, for example by switching a relay or turning a motor. The sensors and actuators are attached to an IoT node (device), usually built around a microcontroller with a radio. A gateway connects local devices to the internet and can translate between protocols, for example from Zigbee or Bluetooth to Wi-Fi or Ethernet, and can filter or aggregate data. The network carries the data, and a cloud or server platform stores and analyses it. Finally, an application or user interface, such as a mobile app or dashboard, lets people see the data and send commands. In home automation, a motion sensor in a room sends an event through a hub (gateway) to the cloud, and a rule turns on the light.

chunks.title: Layered IoT architectures
chunks.content: IoT architectures are often described in layers. The basic three-layer architecture has a perception layer, a network layer and an application layer. The perception layer (also called the sensing or device layer) contains sensors and actuators that collect data from the physical world. The network layer transmits that data to other devices and servers using technologies such as Wi-Fi, cellular networks, Zigbee or LoRa. The application layer delivers services to users, such as a smart home app or a smart city service. A five-layer architecture adds a processing layer (middleware) between the network and application layers to store, analyse and process large amounts of data, and a business layer on top that manages the whole system, including business models and user privacy.

chunks.title: Communication models and design goals
chunks.content: IoT devices communicate in four common models. In the device-to-device model, devices talk directly to each other, for example a light switch and a bulb using Bluetooth or Zigbee. In the device-to-cloud model, a device connects directly to a cloud service over the internet, for example through Wi-Fi. In the device-to-gateway model, devices connect to a local gateway, such as a smartphone or hub, which forwards data to the cloud. In the back-end data-sharing model, data collected in one cloud service is shared with other authorised services so they can combine and analyse it. Design goals for IoT systems include low power consumption, low cost per device, scalability, reliability, security and privacy by design, and interoperability between devices from different vendors.

chunks.title: MQTT basics
chunks.content: MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) is a lightweight messaging protocol designed for constrained devices and unreliable networks. It uses a publish/subscribe model: clients do not send messages directly to each other but to a central server called a broker. A client that sends data publishes a message to a topic, a text string such as home/livingroom/temperature, and the broker forwards the message to every client that has subscribed to that topic. Topics are hierarchical, with levels separated by slashes. Subscribers can use wildcards: the plus sign (+) matches exactly one level, so home/+/temperature matches home/kitchen/temperature, and the hash sign (#) matches all remaining levels and must be the last character, so home/# matches every topic under home. MQTT runs over TCP; the default port is 1883, and 8883 is used for MQTT over TLS.

chunks.title: MQTT quality of service and session features
chunks.content: MQTT offers three Quality of Service (QoS) levels for delivering a message. QoS 0 means at most once: the message is sent once without acknowledgement, so it may be lost. QoS 1 means at least once: the sender keeps the message until it receives a PUBACK, so the message arrives but may be duplicated. QoS 2 means exactly once: a four-step handshake (PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP) makes sure the message arrives once, at the cost of more overhead. A retained message is stored by the broker for its topic and sent immediately to new subscribers, so they get the last known value. The Last Will and Testament is a message the client registers when it connects; the broker publishes it if the client disconnects unexpectedly. The keep-alive interval tells the broker how long the client may stay silent; the client sends PINGREQ packets to show it is still connected.

chunks.title: CoAP
chunks.content: CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) is a web transfer protocol for constrained devices and networks, standardised by the IETF in RFC 7252. Like HTTP it follows the REST style: resources are identified by URIs and accessed with the methods GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, and responses use codes similar to HTTP, such as 2.05 Content or 4.04 Not Found. Unlike HTTP, CoAP runs over UDP, by default on port 5683, and uses a compact 4-byte fixed header to save bandwidth and energy. Because UDP is unreliable, CoAP has its own message types: Confirmable (CON) messages must be acknowledged with an Acknowledgement (ACK) and are retransmitted if no ACK arrives; Non-confirmable (NON) messages are not acknowledged; a Reset (RST) message indicates that a received message could not be processed. With the Observe option, a client can register interest in a resource and the server sends notifications whenever it changes.

questions.content: What does each IoT device need so that it can be found and addressed on a network?
options: A unique identity such as an IP address or device ID
A large colour touch screen for local user input
A permanent wired connection to the electricity grid
A full desktop operating system such as Windows
questions.explanation: Each thing needs a unique identity, such as an IP address or device ID, so that it can be found and addressed.

questions.content: Which term describes IoT devices that have little memory, low processing power and run on batteries?
questions.explanation: Devices with little memory, low processing power and battery power are called constrained devices.

questions.content: Which component lets an IoT device act on the physical world, for example by opening a valve?
questions.explanation: Actuators such as motors, valves or switches act on the physical world; sensors only measure it.

questions.content: What is predictive maintenance in industrial IoT?
options: Replacing every machine on a fixed yearly schedule
Repairing machines only after they have broken down
Buying spare machines in case one of them fails
Using machine sensor data to predict failures early
questions.explanation: Sensors measure vibration and temperature so failures can be predicted before they happen.

questions.content: In smart agriculture, which sensor tells an irrigation system when crops need water?
questions.explanation: Soil moisture sensors tell the irrigation system when to water crops, which saves water.

questions.content: What does interoperability mean for IoT devices?
options: Devices can run for years on a single battery
Devices from different vendors can work together
Devices can encrypt every message that they send
Devices can be installed without any network
questions.explanation: Interoperability is the ability of devices from different vendors, protocols and data formats to work together.

questions.content: Why are many IoT devices easy for attackers to take over?
options: They always use the newest and strongest encryption
They are never connected to the public internet at all
They often keep default passwords and rarely get updates
They are protected by a powerful firewall in the cloud
questions.explanation: Many devices ship with default passwords and rarely get software updates, so attackers can take them over.

questions.content: A smart thermostat measures room temperature and switches the heater on when the room gets cold. Which two IoT capabilities does it use?
questions.explanation: It senses the temperature (sensor) and acts on the heater (actuator).

questions.content: A smart-city network has thousands of sensors from different vendors; some sleep to save energy and new ones are added every month. Which pair of IoT characteristics does this show?
questions.explanation: Devices from many vendors show heterogeneity; devices that sleep, join and leave show dynamic change.

questions.content: A hospital wants to watch a patient's heart rate at home and alert the doctor if it becomes dangerous. Which IoT application area is this?
questions.explanation: Wearable devices that track heart rate and alert doctors remotely are a healthcare (remote monitoring) use.

questions.content: A city wants its street lights to use less energy late at night when roads are empty. Which IoT solution fits best?
options: Replacing all street lights with brighter bulbs
Switching every street light off for the whole night
Lights with motion sensors that dim when nobody is near
Asking residents to report broken lights by email
questions.explanation: Smart street lights dim when roads are empty, saving energy without leaving roads dark.

questions.content: A company buys smart locks from vendor A and a hub from vendor B, but the hub cannot control the locks because they use different protocols. Which IoT challenge is this?
questions.explanation: Devices from different vendors using different protocols that cannot work together is an interoperability problem.

questions.content: A fitness band records sleep times and location all day and uploads them to the cloud. Which concern does this raise most directly?
questions.explanation: Wearables collect personal data about people's habits and health, which is a privacy concern.

questions.content: Why do battery-powered IoT sensors usually sleep most of the time and wake up only to send data?
options: To get more processing power from the CPU
To save energy so the battery lasts longer
To make the radio signal travel much further
To store more readings in their small memory
questions.explanation: Energy is limited for battery-powered devices, so they sleep most of the time to save it.

questions.content: Explain what the Internet of Things is and what an object needs in order to become part of it.

rubric.text: Things exchange data over a network (any one of: collect data, send data, share data, exchange data).
What an object needs (both needed: sensors; network connectivity).
Each thing has a unique identity

questions.explanation: Model answer: The Internet of Things is a network of physical things that collect and exchange data over the internet. An object needs sensors, software and network connectivity. It also needs a unique identity, such as an IP address.

questions.content: Describe how IoT is used in healthcare and in industry, and give the benefit of each.

rubric.text: Healthcare use of IoT (any one of: wearables track heart rate or blood glucose, doctors are alerted remotely).
Industry: sensors on machines measure vibration or temperature
Industry benefit (any one of: failures predicted before they happen, fewer breakdowns, less downtime).

questions.explanation: Model answer: In healthcare, wearable devices track a patient's heart rate or blood glucose and alert doctors remotely when something is wrong. In industry, sensors on machines measure vibration and temperature, so the company can predict failures before they happen and repair the machine in time.

questions.content: Explain why security and privacy are serious problems for IoT devices used in homes.

rubric.text: Devices are easy to break into (any one of: default passwords, weak passwords, rarely updated).
Attackers can take the devices over (any one of: hijack, control the device, use it in a botnet).
Sensors collect personal data about people (any one of: habits, health, daily life).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Many home IoT devices ship with default passwords and rarely get software updates, so attackers can take them over and use them in a botnet. Privacy is also at risk, because cameras, sensors and wearables collect personal data about people's habits and health.

questions.content: IoT devices and systems are often described as constrained, heterogeneous and dynamic. Explain what each of these three characteristics means.

rubric.text: Constrained: devices have limited resources (any one of: little memory, low processing power, battery power).
Heterogeneous: devices differ from each other (any one of: many vendors, different hardware, different protocols).
Dynamic: the set of devices keeps changing (any one of: devices join, leave, move, go offline).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Constrained means that many devices have little memory and low processing power and run on batteries. Heterogeneous means that the devices come from many vendors with different hardware and protocols. Dynamic means that devices join, leave or move all the time, so the system keeps changing.

questions.content: A farm wants to use less water for irrigation. Describe an IoT solution: which device measures the field, which device acts on the water supply, and what rule the system follows.

rubric.text: Soil moisture sensors measure the field
An actuator such as a valve or pump controls the water
Rule: water only when the soil is dry or below a threshold
Benefit: less water is used

questions.explanation: Model answer: Soil moisture sensors are placed in the fields to measure how wet the soil is. A valve on the water pipe is the actuator that the system opens or closes. The rule is to open the valve only when the soil is dry, so the farm saves water.

questions.content: A city plans to install 100,000 IoT sensors from several vendors, most of them running on batteries. For each of these three challenges — security, interoperability and energy — suggest one concrete way to handle it. Also explain why energy matters so much for this project.

rubric.text: Security: one concrete protection (any one of: unique or strong passwords, regular updates, encryption).
Interoperability: require open standards or use gateways that translate protocols
Energy: one way to save power (any one of: low-power hardware or radios, sleep most of the time, energy harvesting).
Why energy matters: batteries are hard to service at this scale (any one of: replacing or recharging 100,000 batteries is slow, costly, impractical).

questions.explanation: Model answer: For security, every sensor should get a unique password and regular security updates. For interoperability, the city should require open standards or use gateways that translate between protocols. For energy, the sensors should use low-power radios and sleep most of the time, waking up only to send data. Energy matters so much because replacing 100,000 batteries would be slow and expensive.

questions.content: Which IoT component connects local devices to the internet and can translate between protocols?
questions.explanation: A gateway connects local devices to the internet and can translate, for example, from Zigbee to Wi-Fi.

questions.content: What is an IoT node usually built around?
questions.explanation: An IoT node is usually built around a microcontroller with a radio.

questions.content: In an IoT system, what is the main job of the cloud or server platform?
options: To store and analyse data from the devices
To measure the room temperature directly
To physically switch the lights on and off
To supply power to battery-powered devices
questions.explanation: The cloud or server platform stores and analyses the data; sensors measure and actuators act.

questions.content: What are the three layers of the basic IoT architecture?
questions.explanation: The basic three-layer IoT architecture has a perception layer, a network layer and an application layer.

questions.content: Which layer of the three-layer IoT architecture contains the sensors and actuators?
questions.explanation: The perception (sensing) layer contains the sensors and actuators.

questions.content: Which layer does the five-layer IoT architecture add between the network and application layers?
questions.explanation: The five-layer architecture adds a processing layer (middleware) between the network and application layers.

questions.content: In which IoT communication model do devices talk directly to each other, for example a switch and a bulb over Bluetooth?
questions.explanation: In the device-to-device model, devices communicate directly with each other.

questions.content: In a home automation system, a motion sensor detects a person and the hall light turns on. What is the role of the light?
options: An actuator that acts on a command
A gateway that links two networks
A broker that routes the messages
questions.explanation: The light changes the physical world when it receives a command, so it is an actuator.

questions.content: Smart bulbs in a house use Zigbee, but the cloud service can only be reached over Wi-Fi. Which component solves this?
options: A second Zigbee bulb next to the Wi-Fi router
A larger battery inside every one of the bulbs
A hub that translates between Zigbee and Wi-Fi
A mobile app that shows the status of the bulbs
questions.explanation: A gateway (hub) connects local devices to the internet and translates between protocols.

questions.content: A team is choosing between Wi-Fi, LoRa and cellular to send sensor data to a server. Which layer of the three-layer architecture are they designing?
questions.explanation: The network layer transmits data using technologies such as Wi-Fi, cellular networks, Zigbee or LoRa.

questions.content: A system must store and analyse terabytes of sensor data before showing results in an app. In the five-layer architecture, which layer does this work?
questions.explanation: The processing layer (middleware) stores, analyses and processes large amounts of data.

questions.content: A smart parking app shows drivers where the free parking spaces are. Which layer of the IoT architecture does the app belong to?
questions.explanation: The application layer delivers services, such as a smart parking app, to users.

questions.content: A fitness band sends data via Bluetooth to the owner's phone, and the phone uploads it to the cloud. Which communication model is this?
questions.explanation: The phone acts as a local gateway that forwards the band's data to the cloud.

questions.content: A thermostat company shares its users' energy data, with their permission, with the electricity provider's platform. Which communication model is this?
questions.explanation: Data collected in one cloud service is shared with another authorised service: back-end data sharing.

questions.content: Explain what sensors, actuators and a gateway each do in an IoT system.

rubric.text: Sensors measure physical quantities
Actuators change the physical world
A gateway links local devices to the internet (any one of: connects them to the internet, translates protocols, forwards their data).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Sensors measure the physical world, for example temperature. Actuators change it, for example by switching a relay. A gateway connects the local devices to the internet and translates between protocols such as Zigbee and Wi-Fi.

questions.content: In the three-layer IoT architecture, which layer is at the bottom and which is at the top? Describe what the bottom layer does.

rubric.text: The lowest layer is the perception layer
The top layer is the application layer
The bottom layer collects data from the physical world (any one of: with sensors, with actuators, senses the environment).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The lowest layer is the perception layer. It uses sensors and actuators to collect data from the physical world. The top layer is the application layer, which delivers services to users.

questions.content: Explain the difference between the device-to-cloud and the device-to-gateway communication models.

rubric.text: Device-to-cloud: the device connects directly to a cloud service
Device-to-gateway (both needed: a local gateway such as a hub or phone; it forwards the data onward to the cloud).

questions.explanation: Model answer: In the device-to-cloud model, the device connects directly to a cloud service over the internet, for example through Wi-Fi. In the device-to-gateway model, the device connects to a local hub or smartphone, which forwards the data to the cloud.

questions.content: Explain why low power consumption and scalability are important design goals for IoT systems.

rubric.text: Low power: many devices run on batteries for a long time
Scalability: a system may grow very large (any one of: millions of devices, large volumes of data).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Low power consumption matters because many devices run on batteries that must last for years. Scalability matters because a system may grow to millions of devices that produce large volumes of data.

questions.content: Design a home automation system that turns on the hall light when someone enters at night. Describe the components and map them to the three architecture layers.

rubric.text: A motion sensor detects the person
A smart bulb or relay is the actuator
The network layer carries the data (any one of: via the hub, via the gateway, over Zigbee or Wi-Fi).
Perception layer mapping (both needed: the motion sensor; the smart bulb or relay).
The rule runs in the application layer

questions.explanation: Model answer: A motion sensor detects a person, and a smart bulb is the actuator that switches the light. The sensor and the bulb belong to the perception layer. They talk to a hub over Zigbee, and the network layer carries the data to the cloud. The rule that turns on the light at night runs in the application layer.

questions.content: Describe the five-layer IoT architecture layer by layer, and explain what the two extra layers add compared with the three-layer model.

rubric.text: Perception layer: sensors collect data
Network layer: transmits the data
Processing layer: handles large amounts of data (any one of: stores, analyses, processes).
Application layer: delivers services to users
Business layer: manages the whole system (any one of: overall management, business models, privacy).

questions.explanation: Model answer: The perception layer has sensors and actuators that collect data. The network layer transmits the data. The processing layer, or middleware, stores and analyses large amounts of data. The application layer delivers services to users. The business layer manages the whole system, including business models and privacy.

questions.content: Which messaging model does MQTT use?
questions.explanation: MQTT uses a publish/subscribe model with a central broker.

questions.content: In MQTT, what is the server that receives messages and forwards them to subscribers called?
questions.explanation: Clients send messages to a central server called a broker, which forwards them to subscribers.

questions.content: What is the default port for MQTT without TLS?
questions.explanation: MQTT uses port 1883 by default and 8883 over TLS; 5683 is the CoAP port.

questions.content: Which MQTT QoS level delivers a message exactly once?
questions.explanation: QoS 2 uses a four-step handshake to deliver a message exactly once; there is no QoS 3.

questions.content: What does the broker do with a retained message?
options: Stores it and sends it to new subscribers of the topic
Deletes it after the first subscriber reads it
Sends it back only to the client that published it
Hides it until the publisher connects again
questions.explanation: A retained message is stored for its topic and sent immediately to new subscribers.

questions.content: Which transport protocol does CoAP use by default?
questions.explanation: Unlike HTTP, CoAP runs over UDP, by default on port 5683.

questions.content: Which CoAP message type must be acknowledged by the receiver?
questions.explanation: Confirmable messages must be acknowledged with an ACK and are retransmitted if no ACK arrives.

questions.content: A client subscribes to the topic home/+/temperature. Which published topic will it receive?
questions.explanation: The plus sign matches exactly one level, so only home/<one level>/temperature matches.

questions.content: Which subscription receives every message published under home, at any depth?
questions.explanation: The hash sign matches all remaining levels and must be the last character.

questions.content: A sensor sends a temperature reading every second, and losing one reading does not matter. Which QoS level is the most efficient choice?
questions.explanation: QoS 0 (at most once) has no acknowledgement overhead; an occasional lost reading is acceptable here.

questions.content: A door lock must receive the 'unlock' command once and only once, even on an unreliable network. Which QoS level fits?
questions.explanation: Only QoS 2 guarantees exactly-once delivery; QoS 1 may deliver the command twice.

questions.content: A monitoring app wants to know when a sensor goes offline unexpectedly. Which MQTT feature should the sensor set when it connects?
questions.explanation: The broker publishes the Last Will message if the client disconnects unexpectedly.

questions.content: A client sends a CoAP GET request for /temperature and the resource exists. Which response code is typical?
questions.explanation: 2.05 Content returns the resource; 4.04 means it does not exist.

questions.content: A dashboard must be told every time a sensor's value changes, without sending repeated GET requests. Which CoAP feature helps?
questions.explanation: With the Observe option, the server sends notifications whenever the resource changes.

questions.content: Explain how messages travel from one client to another in MQTT.

rubric.text: Messages go through a central broker
A client publishes a message to a topic
The broker forwards the message to the subscribers

questions.explanation: Model answer: In MQTT, clients do not send messages directly to each other. A client publishes a message to a topic on a central broker, and the broker forwards it to every client that has subscribed to that topic.

questions.content: Compare MQTT QoS 0 and QoS 1.

rubric.text: QoS 0 (both needed: delivered at most once or without acknowledgement; the message may be lost).
QoS 1 (both needed: delivered at least once or acknowledged with PUBACK; the message may be duplicated).

questions.explanation: Model answer: QoS 0 means at most once: the message is sent without acknowledgement, so it may be lost. QoS 1 means at least once: the sender keeps the message until it gets a PUBACK, so it arrives but may be duplicated.

questions.content: Why does CoAP define both Confirmable and Non-confirmable messages?

rubric.text: CoAP runs over unreliable UDP
Confirmable messages (both needed: acknowledged with an ACK; retransmitted if no ACK arrives).
Non-confirmable messages are not acknowledged, which saves resources (any one of: energy, bandwidth, fewer messages).

questions.explanation: Model answer: CoAP runs over UDP, which is unreliable. Confirmable messages must be acknowledged with an ACK and are retransmitted if no ACK arrives. Non-confirmable messages are not acknowledged, which saves energy and bandwidth for data that can be lost.

questions.content: Give two ways in which CoAP is similar to HTTP and one way in which it is different.

rubric.text: Both follow the REST style: resources identified by URIs
Like HTTP, CoAP uses requests with methods or codes (any one of: methods such as GET or POST, similar response codes).
CoAP differs in transport or size (any one of: runs over UDP instead of TCP, small 4-byte header).

questions.explanation: Model answer: Like HTTP, CoAP follows the REST style and identifies resources with URIs. It also uses methods such as GET and POST and response codes similar to HTTP. Unlike HTTP, CoAP runs over UDP instead of TCP.

questions.content: Design the MQTT messaging for a smart greenhouse with a temperature sensor and a fan in each of three rooms. Give example topics, a subscription that lets one dashboard read all rooms, and the delivery guarantee you would use for sensor data and for fan commands.

rubric.text: All messages go through one broker
Each room has its own topic level (any one of: greenhouse/<room>/temperature, one topic per room).
The dashboard subscribes with the single-level wildcard (any one of: +, plus sign, matches one level).
Sensor data: QoS 0 (at most once)
Fan commands: QoS 1 or QoS 2

questions.explanation: Model answer: All devices connect to one broker. Each room publishes to its own topic, for example greenhouse/room1/temperature, and each fan subscribes to a command topic such as greenhouse/room1/fan. The dashboard subscribes to greenhouse/+/temperature, where the plus sign matches one level, so it gets all rooms. Sensor readings use QoS 0, because a lost reading is replaced a second later. Fan commands use QoS 1, so a command is not lost.

questions.content: A battery-powered sensor network must choose between MQTT and CoAP. Compare the two protocols and recommend one for a device that only answers occasional requests from a server.

rubric.text: MQTT runs over TCP
MQTT needs a broker
CoAP is light on the network (any one of: runs over UDP, small 4-byte header).
CoAP follows the REST style
Recommends CoAP

questions.explanation: Model answer: MQTT runs over TCP and needs a broker, and devices keep a connection open. CoAP runs over UDP with a small 4-byte header, which saves energy. CoAP follows the REST style, where a server reads a resource with GET. For a device that only answers occasional requests, I recommend CoAP, because it needs no broker and no open TCP connection.
